Tic-tac-toe: a table of values

The agent keeps one number for every board it has seen: its estimate of how the game will end from there, on a scale from 0 (a loss) to 1 (a win). It moves to the board with the highest number. After each move it nudges the number for its previous board towards the number for its new board. That is the whole learning rule.

You are O. The agent is X and moves first. Click a square to play. Find a way to beat it, then play the same moves again.

The maths

This is S&B's opening example (§1.5). Score a win as $1$, a draw as $\tfrac12$ and a loss as $0$. Let $V(s)$ be the agent's estimate of its expected score from board $s$, where $s$ is a board just after the agent's own move. Boards the game has already decided are fixed:

$$V(s) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{X has three in a row} \\ 0 & \text{O has three in a row} \\ \tfrac12 & \text{a draw, or undecided (initial guess)} \end{cases}$$

A known result gets its true value. Every other board starts as a coin flip.

To move, the agent looks at each board it could create and usually picks the one with the highest $V$. With probability $\varepsilon$ it picks a random move instead, to explore. After a greedy move from board $S_t$ to board $S_{t+1}$:

$$V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\big[V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)\big]$$

The previous board's value moves a fraction $\alpha$ of the way towards the value of the board that followed it. Good outcomes leak backwards, one move per game.

When O ends the game, the agent's last board is moved towards $0$. After an exploratory move there is no update: the values estimate how well the agent does when it plays its best, and a deliberate random move says little about that.

The update uses one estimate as the target for another. That idea is called temporal-difference learning, and Lesson 45 makes it precise. S&B count draws as $0$, which makes $V$ a probability of winning; their goal is to beat an imperfect player. Here a draw is $\tfrac12$, so the agent prefers a draw to a loss.

If $\alpha$ shrinks slowly over time, the values converge to the true expected scores against this opponent when the agent plays greedily, and the greedy moves become the best replies to this opponent (S&B §1.5).
